Gram-positive cocci · slides 4–15

Staphylococci

The medically important Gram-positive cocci split by arrangement GP 4: Staphylococcus in clusters (S. aureus, S. epidermidis, S. saprophyticus) and Streptococcus in chains (S. pyogenes Group A, S. agalactiae Group B, S. pneumoniae, viridans streptococci, Enterococcus).

StaphylococciStreptococci GP 5
Clusters (grape-like)Chains or pairs
Catalase +Catalase −
Facultative anaerobesObligate and facultative anaerobes; grow in 5–10% CO2
Grow on ordinary mediumFastidious: need enriched medium such as blood agar
Flora of skin, nose and mucosaFlora of throat, colon, female genital tract
Localized infectionsInfections tend to spread
Resistant to drying and penicillinDelicate, sensitive to penicillin

Three species GP 6 GP 15

  • S. aureus: coagulase positive, the most virulent; the most common cause of bacterial infections, food poisoning and toxic shock syndrome.
  • S. epidermidis: coagulase negative, a major part of skin flora; causes nosocomial device and implant infections (shunts, catheters, artificial heart valves, joints, pacemakers).
  • S. saprophyticus: coagulase negative, occasionally on skin, GI and GU tracts; urinary tract infection in young women.

S. aureus features GP 7: beta hemolytic, heat resistant, salt tolerant (grows in 10–15% NaCl), tolerant of drying, golden yellow pigment, non-spore forming, non-motile.

Virulence factors GP 8

Toxins GP 9

Hemolysins lyse RBCs · leucocidins kill leucocytes · enterotoxins A–E, heat and acid resistant: food poisoning · TSST (enterotoxin F): toxic shock syndrome (rash, desquamation, multi-organ failure) · exfoliative toxins A and B: scalded skin syndrome in young children.

Enzymes and surface GP 10 GP 11

Catalase · coagulase · β-lactamase (resistance to β-lactams). Protein A: antiphagocytic · clumping factor: clumping in plasma, blocks phagocytosis · slime layer: blocks chemotaxis and phagocytosis, attaches to artificial surfaces.

Diseases GP 12 GP 13

  • Non-invasive: food poisoning from ingested enterotoxin.
  • Cutaneous: scalded skin syndrome, impetigo, folliculitis, furuncle (boil), abscess.
  • Systemic: toxic shock syndrome, bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis.

Lab diagnosis of S. aureus GP 14: wound swab, pus or blood → Gram stain → blood agar (beta hemolysis), nutrient agar (golden pigment) → catalase +, coagulase +, mannitol fermentation (yellow).

Golden, Salty, ToughS. aureus: golden pigment, grows in 10–15% salt, survives heat and drying.
A to E eat, F is for shockEnterotoxins A–E cause food poisoning; enterotoxin F is TSST.
Catalase separates staph from strep; coagulase separates S. aureus from the other staphylococci. Epidermidis = implants; saprophyticus = urine.

Gram-positive cocci · slides 16–25

Streptococci and enterococci

Gram-positive cocci in pairs or chains, facultative anaerobes GP 17, classified three ways: oxygen requirement, hemolysis on blood agar, and the Lancefield C carbohydrate antigen.

Basis GP 18Groups
OxygenAerobes: streptococci · anaerobes: peptostreptococci
HemolysisAlpha: incomplete, green (S. viridans, S. pneumoniae) · beta: complete · gamma: none (Enterococcus faecalis)
LancefieldSpecific C carbohydrate antigen on the cell wall: groups A to U (21); groups A and B include the main human pathogens

Beta: Group A, S. pyogenes GP 19 GP 20

Infections

Respiratory (strep throat): pharyngitis, tonsillitis, scarlet fever, otitis media, sinusitis. Skin: pyoderma (impetigo), erysipelas, cellulitis (invasive), necrotising fasciitis (flesh eating, invasive).

Late, non-suppurative

Acute rheumatic fever: usually after pharyngitis. Acute glomerulonephritis: usually after pyoderma.

Scarlet fever GP 21: GAS producing pyrogenic exotoxins; fever, generalized rash, desquamation; oral signs in almost all cases: strawberry tongue, Forchheimer spots (fleeting red spots on the soft palate), inflamed uvula.

Lab diagnosis GP 22: throat swab, pus, blood → GPC in chains → beta hemolytic colonies → catalase −, bacitracin sensitive, penicillin sensitive, ASO titre.

Alpha: viridans streptococci GP 23 GP 24

Normal on teeth, throat, colon and female genital tract; lack group-specific carbohydrates, so no Lancefield group; green pigment on blood agar. Clinical: endocarditis, dental caries, pulpitis. The most common causes of pulpitis: alpha hemolytic streptococci and peptostreptococci.

Gamma: enterococci GP 25

Flora of the GIT and lower genital tract; nosocomial, opportunistic. Species: E. faecalis, E. faecium. UTI, wound infection, endocarditis. E. faecalis is named as the main reason for endodontic failure: it resists disinfection agents and causes persistent intra- or extra-radicular infection.

Throat → heart, skin → kidneyRheumatic fever usually follows pharyngitis; glomerulonephritis usually follows pyoderma.
Faecalis fails the root canalE. faecalis survives disinfection and keeps the lesion going.
S. pneumoniae is alpha, not beta. Enterococcus is gamma on GP 18. Forchheimer spots (scarlet fever) are not Koplik spots (measles).

Gram-positive rods · slides 26–33

Classification and the aerobic rods

GP 28SporingNon-sporing
Aerobes or facultativeBacillusLactobacillus, Corynebacterium
AnaerobesClostridiumActinomyces

Lactobacillus GP 30

  • Commensal flora of mucous membranes; keep the acid pH of normal mucosa.
  • Acidogenic: large quantities of lactic acid from carbohydrates. Aciduric: grow and survive at very low pH.
  • Role in caries progression, especially in dentine; a very important cause of advanced dental caries.

Corynebacterium diphtheriae GP 31 GP 32

  • Small, slender, pleomorphic rods in clumps like Chinese letters; non-spore forming. Disease: diphtheria.
  • Droplets, respiratory entry. Strains lysogenized by a bacteriophage make a powerful exotoxin: tissue death and necrosis.
  • Pseudomembrane in the throat may extend and cause suffocation.
  • Toxaemia: the bacilli do not invade; the toxin reaches heart muscle and peripheral nerves through the blood. Neuritis of cranial and peripheral nerves: paralysis, difficulty speaking and swallowing.

Prevention and treatment GP 33

DPT at 2, 4, 6 months; boosters at 1.5 and 5 years. Penicillin; antitoxin for acute cases, given early; respiratory support if needed.

Lacto loves acid, twiceAcidogenic makes it; aciduric lives in it.
Diphtheria toxin is phage-dependent; tetanus toxin is on a plasmid. Diphtheria does not invade: it is toxaemia.

Gram-positive rods · slides 34–40

Clostridia and Actinomyces

Clostridia GP 34: obligate anaerobes (oxygen inhibits growth), Gram-positive, spore-forming rods. Habitat: soil and the intestines of animals and humans. Two diseases GP 35: gas gangrene and tetanus.

GP 36DiseaseVirulence factor
C. perfringensMyonecrosis (gas gangrene), anaerobic cellulitisα toxin (lecithinase): lyses endothelium, RBCs, leucocytes, platelets. Enzymes (DNase, collagenase) liquefy tissue and spread infection.
C. tetaniTetanus: spastic paralysis, lock jaw, painful spasm, convulsions, death by respiratory failureTetanospasmin, encoded on a plasmid

Actinomyces GP 37 GP 38

Grow as branching filaments like fungi, but are true bacteria: Gram-positive type cell wall; no nuclear membrane or mitochondria; killed by antibacterial, not antifungal, drugs. Oral and dental links: cervicofacial actinomycosis, dental caries, dental plaque, dental implant infections.

Cervicofacial actinomycosis GP 39 GP 40

Endogenous (oral flora). Risk factors: untreated caries, extractions, local trauma. Face, neck and mandible: swelling with fibrosis, draining sinus tracts, suppurative. Pus contains yellow sulfur granules (silver stain on GP 40).

Perfringens Pops muscle, Tetani Tightens itGas gangrene versus spastic paralysis.
Actinomyces look like fungi but are bacteria. Clostridia are sporing; Actinomyces are non-sporing.

Mycology · slides 3–11

Fungi: structure, growth and disease

Mycology is the study of fungal infections (mycoses) MY 3. Hyphae are tubular filaments; a mycelium is a mass of branching, interlinking hyphae.

Feature MY 4FungiBacteria
Diameter≈ 4 µm (Candida)≈ 1 µm (Staphylococcus)
NucleusEukaryoticProkaryotic
CytoplasmMitochondria and ERNo mitochondria or ER
Membrane sterolsPresentAbsent (except Mycoplasma)
WallChitinPeptidoglycan
SporesSexual and asexual, for reproductionEndospores for survival
Thermal dimorphismYes (some)No
MetabolismNeed organic carbon; no obligate anaerobesMany need no organic carbon; many obligate anaerobes

Wall, membrane and drug targets MY 5

  • Chitin (polymer of N-acetylglucosamine), not peptidoglycan: so penicillins and cephalosporins do not work.
  • β-glucan (polymer of D-glucose): the target of caspofungin.
  • Ergosterol in the fungal membrane, cholesterol in human membranes: the basis of the selective toxicity of amphotericin B and azoles.

Classification and growth MY 6 MY 7 MY 8

  • By spores: sexual (meiosis) or asexual (mitosis). By growth form: yeasts, molds, dimorphic.
  • Yeasts (Candida albicans): round to oval, unicellular, reproduce by budding, may form pseudohyphae.
  • Molds (dermatophytes): multinucleate cytoplasm in tubular filaments; grow by branching and longitudinal extension.
  • Dimorphic: yeast at 37 °C in tissue, mold at 22 °C in the environment.

Fungal disease MY 9 MY 10 MY 11

Mycoses

Superficial: mucous membranes by yeast (thrush); keratinized tissue by dermatophyte (ringworm). Subcutaneous: implanted environmental spores (mycetoma). Systemic: serious, haematogenous (systemic aspergillosis).

Mycotoxicoses and allergy

Aflatoxin of Aspergillus flavus: carcinogenic, liver cancer. Allergy: inhaled spores, notably Aspergillus fumigatus.

Heat makes yeastBody temperature (37 °C) gives the yeast form; room temperature gives mold.
MY 8 text gives 22 °C for the mold form; the picture on MY 7 labels it 25 °C. Chitin = N-acetylglucosamine; β-glucan = D-glucose.

Mycology · slides 12–15

Candida and oral candidiasis

Candidiasis (candidosis) MY 12: infection with Candida species. Candida albicans gives:

  • Superficial: mucosal thrush (white patches on oral mucosa or vagina; esophageal in the immunocompromised); cutaneous (red weeping areas); chronic mucocutaneous candidosis (face and scalp, first two years, congenital T cell defect).
  • Deep: candidemia spreading to eye, endocardium, meninges, kidney, liver.

Oral thrush MY 13

Multiple white plaques on lips, tongue and palate. Risk: weak immune system (serious disease, cancer treatment). Treatment: antimycotics. Source usually endogenous; cross infection mother to baby and back.

Lab diagnosis MY 14 MY 15

Swab (oral, wound, vaginal, throat) → Gram-positive, spherical to oval, unicellular budding yeasts → culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar → germ tube test: an appendage half the width and 3–4 times the length of the yeast cell; C. albicans is germ tube positive.

Germ tube: thin and longHalf the width, three to four times the length.
Thrush is superficial (mucosal); candidemia is deep. Hairy leukoplakia (EBV) is also white but corrugated with ridges.

Virology · slides 3–10

Virus structure, classification and replication

Structure VI 3: a genome of DNA or RNA, never both; a capsid of repeating capsomers that protects it; in some viruses an envelope, a lipid bilayer from the host cell. A virion is the complete particle.

Classification VI 4 VI 6 VI 7

  • By capsid symmetry: icosahedral (spherical), helical (rod-shaped or coiled), complex.
  • By nucleic acid: DNA or RNA, single or double stranded; ssRNA and dsDNA are commonest in nature.
  • By envelope: enveloped or naked. The envelope is antigenic (viral glycoproteins), from host membranes, and makes the virus more sensitive to heat, drying, detergents and lipid solvents (alcohol, ether).
  • By replication strategy: the Baltimore classification, 7 groups by the pathway from genome to mRNA.
Genome VI 5Families
ssDNA, nakedParvoviridae
dsDNA, nakedAdenoviridae, Papovaviridae
dsDNA, envelopedHepadnaviridae, Herpesviridae, Poxviridae
ss(+)RNA, icosahedral, nakedCaliciviridae, Picornaviridae
ss(+)RNA, envelopedCoronaviridae, Flaviviridae, Retroviridae, Togaviridae
ss(−)RNA, helical, envelopedArena, Bunya, Filo, Orthomyxo, Paramyxo, Rhabdoviridae
dsRNA, nakedReoviridae

Replication cycle VI 9: adsorption → penetration → uncoating → genome replication → assembly → release.

Effects on cells VI 10

Lytic (cytocidal): the cell is killed. Abortive: no progeny. Persistent productive: progeny without killing (HBV). Latent: genome dormant, no progeny (VZV); consequences: reactivation or tumours (transformation, papillomavirus).

A Pen Under A Rubber RoofAdsorption, Penetration, Uncoating, Replication, Assembly, Release.
Enveloped viruses are the weaker ones outside the body. Latent = no progeny; persistent productive = progeny without killing.

Systemic virology · slides 12–22

Herpesviruses

Rash words VI 12: macule (flat, under 1 cm) · papule (raised) · vesicle (fluid-filled).

Herpesviruses VI 13: eight human species; all can go latent after primary infection and reactivate; EBV and HHV-8 are oncogenic; many have oral signs; dsDNA, enveloped, icosahedral.

HSV-1 VI 14HSV-2
SpreadSaliva (kissing)Sexual contact; vertically at birth
PrimaryGingivostomatitisGenital herpes, perinatal disseminated disease
LatencyTrigeminal gangliaSacral ganglia

Reactivation inducers: fever, sunlight, hormonal changes, trauma, stress, immunosuppression.

  • Acute herpetic gingivostomatitis VI 15: vesiculoulcerative lesions of the mouth, to lips, face, nose, eyes; very painful; heal in 7–10 days.
  • Herpetic whitlow: painful infection of one or more fingers; dentists who escaped childhood exposure may catch it from patients.
  • Reactivation VI 16: herpes labialis (cold sores) in the skin supplied by the neurons, or only asymptomatic shedding.

Chickenpox VI 17

Primary VZV. Rash on the trunk first, then face and limbs: macules → vesicles → pustules → crusts, no scar.

Shingles VI 17 VI 18

Reactivated VZV, usually in the immunocompromised (disease, therapy, aging). Unilateral clustered vesicles in a dermatome. About 15% of elderly patients get postherpetic neuralgia.

  • EBV VI 19: droplets (kissing disease); epithelium of oropharynx, nasopharynx, salivary glands → lymph nodes → viremia in the immunosuppressed. Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Oral hairy leukoplakia: white corrugated plaque with hair-like projections.
  • CMV VI 20: secretions (saliva most common), breast milk, transplacental, blood. Congenital infection, asymptomatic infection, infectious mononucleosis (fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly).
  • HHV-8 VI 21: saliva, sex, blood, transplants. Kaposi's sarcoma: malignancy of vascular endothelial cells; reddish to dark purple, flat to nodular; skin, mouth, GIT, lungs.
Virus VI 22LatencyRecurrent
HSV-1Cranial sensory gangliaHerpes labialis, encephalitis, keratitis
HSV-2Lumbar or sacral gangliaHerpes genitalis
VZVCranial or thoracic gangliaZoster
EBVB lymphocytesAsymptomatic shedding
CMVMonocytesAsymptomatic shedding
HHV-8UncertainKaposi's sarcoma
One up top, two down belowHSV-1 in the trigeminal ganglia; HSV-2 in the sacral ganglia.
B for Barr, M for MegaEBV latent in B lymphocytes; cytomegalovirus in monocytes.
Chickenpox starts on the trunk; measles starts on the head. Hairy leukoplakia is EBV, not Candida.

Systemic virology · slides 23–30

Blood-borne viruses: HIV, HBV and HCV

HIV VI 24: single-stranded RNA, enveloped retrovirus. Target: CD4 T-helper cells, which it kills, causing recurrent infections and malignancies. Macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells and neurons are infected but not destroyed: they are reservoirs.

Transmission VI 25

Sexual · blood and blood products · vertical (pregnancy, childbirth, breast feeding).

Prevention

Screen blood · sterilize (the envelope is destroyed by organic solvents) · no shared needles · no vaccine yet.

Stage VI 26What happens
Acute HIVFlu-like symptoms days to weeks after infection; symptomatic phase 7–10 days
Chronic HIVLatent or asymptomatic; can last several years. Latency comes from rapid mutation and depletion of CD4 and CD8 cells
AIDSCD4 below 200 cells/mm³; opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining conditions

Oral signs of HIV VI 27 VI 28: fungal: candidiasis · viral: hairy leukoplakia (EBV), Kaposi's sarcoma (HHV-8), herpetic stomatitis · bacterial: oral TB · malignancy: Kaposi, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

HBV and HCV VI 29: blood, vertical, and sexual (HBV). Infect hepatocytes → cirrhosis → liver failure and death; may give hepatocellular carcinoma.

VI 30HBVHCV
Incubation1.5 months2 weeks
BothFever, anorexia, vomiting; jaundice, dark urine, pale stool
CourseSymptoms more severe; chronic carriers mostly asymptomatic; HCC uncommon, years later80% asymptomatic; chronic active hepatitis → cirrhosis, failure, HCC
Under 200, AIDS has begunThe CD4 threshold for AIDS.
The incubation periods on VI 30 (HBV 1.5 months, HCV 2 weeks) are the lecture's figures; textbooks give longer ones. Its “HCC uncommon” for HBV is also the slide’s wording; textbooks rate HBV as a major cause of HCC. Answer with the slide. Sexual spread is marked for HBV.

Systemic virology · slides 31–35

Coxsackie, mumps, measles and HPV

  • Coxsackieviruses VI 32: herpangina (fever, sore throat, dysphagia, anorexia, stiff neck; grey-white papulovesicles ringed in red on the palate); hand, foot and mouth disease (mainly A16); aseptic meningitis.
  • Mumps VI 33: acute disease of children; parotitis, one or both; other salivary glands may enlarge; droplets.
  • Measles VI 34: highly infectious; children and non-immune adults; aerosol. Prodrome: fever and the 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis). 2–3 days later Koplik spots (bluish-white pinpoint spots on bright red mucosa), then a macular rash from the head down. Not infectious soon after the rash appears.
  • HPV VI 35: infects squamous epithelium, including the mouth; direct contact (kissing, orogenital). Warts around or inside the mouth like small cauliflower masses; strongly associated with oropharyngeal cancer.
3 Cs then KoplikCough, coryza, conjunctivitis; then Koplik spots; then the rash from the head down.
Herpangina (coxsackie): grey-white papulovesicles ringed in red on the palate, with fever and a stiff neck. Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1): very painful vesicles of the gums and the whole mouth, spreading to the lips and face.

Memory aids

Hooks, numbers and traps

Read these out loud, then test yourself in the Flashcards. The key-facts grid is your last-hour sheet.

How questions catch you

Trick 1Catalase or coagulase?

Catalase splits staph (+) from strep (−). Coagulase splits S. aureus (+) from the other staphylococci.

Trick 2Swapped partners

Pharyngitis → rheumatic fever; pyoderma → glomerulonephritis. HSV-1 trigeminal; HSV-2 sacral. EBV B cells; CMV monocytes.

Trick 3Which spots?

Forchheimer: red, soft palate, scarlet fever. Koplik: bluish-white on red buccal mucosa, measles.

Trick 4Which white lesion?

Thrush: Candida plaques. Hairy leukoplakia: EBV, corrugated. Pseudomembrane: diphtheria.

Trick 5Looks like, but is

Actinomyces branch like fungi but are bacteria. Candida is Gram positive but is a fungus.

Trick 6Direction words

Enveloped viruses are MORE sensitive. Chickenpox starts on the trunk; measles on the head.

Objectives

Can you do what each lecture says you should?

66 questions written against the learning objectives printed at the start of each lecture (GP 3, GP 27, MY 2, VI 2), numbered by objective. Every answer shows why and the slide it comes from. Keys a–d or 1–4 answer, T and F for true/false, Enter goes next.

The objectives
  • Cocci objectives: 1. List Gram-positive bacteria by shape and arrangement · 2. General features of virulent and less virulent staphylococci · 3. Pathogenesis and clinical significance of coagulase-positive and coagulase-negative staphylococci · 4. Classify streptococci by hemolysis and Lancefield group · 5. Clinical importance of Group A streptococci, enterococci and viridans streptococci
  • Rods objectives: 1. Outline the classification of Gram-positive rods · 2. Aerobic rods: lactobacilli and Corynebacterium diphtheriae · 3. Anaerobic rods: C. perfringens against C. tetani, and Actinomyces
